characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: The Technical Feasibility Strategy guides the design and implementation of non-production demonstrators to prove platform-neutral or fallback authentication options. It defines scope, acceptable methods, risk controls, and budget envelopes, and tracks progress toward credible demonstrations. Its primary objectives are to validate architectural assumptions, quantify risks, and produce tangible evidence to inform policy and procurement discussions. Key success metrics include the number and quality of demonstrators (e.g., FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback), a published feasibility report, and a financing plan supporting later phases.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: The strongest positive interactions are with Policy Advocacy Strategy and Coalition Building Strategy, as demonstrable technical results provide credible leverage for advocating platform neutrality. It also supports EU Standards Engagement Strategy by supplying real-world inputs for standardization discussions.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Trade-offs include resource demands and potential scope creep; focusing on demonstrators can delay procurement negotiations if budgets are stretched. It may constrain Procurement Influence Strategy when demonstrator complexity clashes with timetables, and could complicate EU Standards Engagement Strategy if fast results bias national standards away from Europe-wide alignment.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: Policy Advocacy Strategy shapes the policy and procurement dimensions of the project. It reframes resilience, continuity of service, supplier concentration risk, and procurement neutrality into formal policy proposals, stakeholder engagements, and messaging. It directly aims to influence Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and related authorities, with success measured by policy proposals submitted, formal responses secured, and inclusion of platform-neutral concepts in AltID or procurement discussions. The lever also prioritizes privacy, democratic accountability, and continuity, balancing to avoid capture. It iterates with Coalition Building Strategy to align messages.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Policy advocacy gains credibility when grounded in demonstrator results; it synergizes with Coalition Building Strategy to broaden messaging and with EU Standards Engagement Strategy to align national aims with Europe-wide requirements. This fosters a policy narrative that supports resilience, continuity, and platform neutrality across public procurement.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Policy advocacy can invite regulatory capture risk and potentially alienate privacy advocates if messaging is overly narrow. It may constrain Coalition Building Strategy by forcing a fixed policy stance, and could conflict with EU Standards Engagement Strategy if national messaging lags EU alignment.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: Coalition Building Strategy expands the base of supporters beyond security experts to civil society, privacy advocates, academics, and contingency-planning stakeholders. It coordinates outreach, surfaces blockers, and maintains a shared advocacy rhythm. Its objectives are to grow breadth and coherence of the advocacy front, accelerate decision momentum, and strengthen political leverage. Metrics include the number of engaged organizations, documented positions, and a consensus-ready coalition output that can accompany policy and procurement discussions. It also emphasizes inclusive governance and transparent decision gates to maintain momentum.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Expanding the coalition amplifies policy and technical narratives, boosting credibility for Policy Advocacy Strategy and making Procurement Influence Strategy more effective through a united front. It also creates shared data sources and messaging guidelines that help align comments to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, MitID operator, and EU discussions.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Coalition breadth risks slower decision-making and internal dilution of messaging; divergent priorities can undermine a unified stance. It may constrain Policy Advocacy Strategy if consensus drifts toward lowest-common-denominator positions, and could complicate Procurement Influence Strategy when vendor influences pull toward narrower, faster agendas.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: Procurement Influence Strategy focuses on embedding platform-neutrality and certified fallback authentication requirements into procurement documents and processes. It aims to diversify suppliers, reduce dependency on single platform ecosystems, and align contract terms with resilience objectives. Success is measured by the inclusion of explicit platform-neutral and fallback language, shorter procurement cycles, and broader supplier participation, enabling faster scaling while preserving security and privacy standards. It also requires governance processes to ensure ongoing sunset clauses for platform dependencies and regular reviews with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: It strengthens the Coalition Building Strategy by creating shared procurement narratives and gives Policy Advocacy Strategy concrete levers to press for change; demonstrator results from Technical Feasibility Strategy inform procurement specs. This synergy accelerates supplier diversification and reduces lock-in while maintaining security guarantees.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Procurement language can be gamed or challenged by incumbents; overly prescriptive terms risk litigation or delays. It may constrain Technical Feasibility Strategy if demonstrator choices become entangled with contract language, and could slow EU Standards Engagement Strategy if national terms diverge from EU expectations.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: EU Standards Engagement Strategy coordinates formal input to European bodies and aligns national work with the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, NSIS, and eIDAS2 expectations. It aims to achieve measurable interoperability and reduced lock-in, with success metrics including contribution to EU debates, alignment with Wallet requirements, and concrete signals shaping national procurement and policy to accommodate platform-neutral fallback paths. It leverages findings from Technical Feasibility Strategy, Policy Advocacy Strategy, and Procurement Influence Strategy to influence standards work, while managing risks of vendor capture through balanced stakeholder input.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: It aligns national work with Europe-wide objectives, amplifying Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy through EU channels and ensuring Coalition Building Strategy has credible, interoperable targets. This engagement also provides legitimacy for platform-neutral approaches in national debates and procurement processes.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: EU standards engagement can be slow and susceptible to vendor influence; it may constrain national procurement timetables and create tensions if EU requirements demand compromises that conflict with Phase three ambitions. It can also divert resources from domestic policy advocacy efforts and place pressure on coalition messaging.
